interest: This file offers valuable insights into the social, legal, and institutional landscape of early post-war occupied Japan, particularly regarding how private groups, diaspora populations, and civic bodies sought legitimacy under Allied occupation. Most remarkably, it documents the existence and constitution of the Peruvian Nisei Association of Japan, illuminating the precarious legal status and self-organization of Latin American Nisei stranded in post-war Japan who sought consular protection and communication with the Peruvian government through U.S. diplomatic channels while carefully codifying their strict neutrality in Japanese politics. Furthermore, the file sheds light on early post-surrender attempts by Japanese elites—via the Central Liaison Office—to establish the Peace Construction Research Institute to self-investigate the causes of Japanese military aggression and document war destruction, and illustrates SCAP's diplomatic policy of discouraging such retrospective academic projects prior to the conclusion of a formal peace treaty. Finally, it highlights the proliferation of unauthorized private claims organizations soliciting fees from Allied veterans and the deferential rhetoric adopted by Japanese commercial figures attempting to cultivate American favor and revive foreign trade.
keywords: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
overview: This State Department decimal file (894.43, Japan: Societies) spans August 1946 to March 1948 and consists of correspondence, diplomatic despatches, charters, and instructions relating to various private, commercial, and research associations operating in or concerned with occupied Japan. The file covers four distinct subjects: congressional and State Department correspondence regarding 'Liberated Military Personnel (Japan)', an unauthorized Washington-based entity soliciting claims from former prisoners of war; the establishment in Tokyo of the Peruvian Nisei Association of Japan (Asociación de Niseis Peruanos del Japón), whose founding statutes were transmitted via U.S. diplomatic channels in Yokohama and Washington to the Peruvian government in Lima; an appeal from Shujiro Iwasaki, president of the Tokyo International Club, to President Harry S. Truman seeking American guidance and commercial ties to foster peaceful trade and spread democracy; and a proposal submitted through the Japanese Central Liaison Office to establish the Peace Construction Research Institute to investigate the historical causes and material losses of Japan's recent wars, which U.S. occupation authorities deemed premature prior to a formal peace treaty.

subfiles.about: Representative Walt Horan requests information and an official statement from the State Department regarding a private group named Liberated Military Personnel (Japan).
subfiles.summary: Representative Walt Horan of Washington State writes to the Department of State inquiring about the legitimacy of an organization known as Liberated Military Personnel (Japan), based in Washington, D.C. Horan notes that he received an inquiry about the organization and requests an official evaluation from the Department. The letter is written on House of Representatives Committee on Appropriations stationery listing the counties of his congressional district and staff members.
subfiles.title: Letter from Representative Walt Horan to the State Department regarding Liberated Military Personnel (Japan)

subfiles.about: The Acting Secretary of State informs Representative Horan that the government does not sponsor private groups soliciting military claims against Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Acting Secretary of State acknowledges Representative Horan's August 9 letter regarding the Liberated Military Personnel (Japan) organization. He explains that due to numerous similar inquiries, the Departments of State, War, and Navy have drafted a joint press release (No. 576) warning the public that the government does not endorse or sponsor any private committees soliciting claims. The Departments recommend that veterans and claimants present their claims directly through official military or diplomatic channels rather than private organizations.
subfiles.title: Letter from the Acting Secretary of State to Representative Walt Horan regarding Claims Solicitation Organizations

subfiles.about: Consul General U. Alexis Johnson transmits the articles of association of the newly formed Peruvian Nisei Association of Japan for forwarding to the Government of Peru.
subfiles.from: U. Alexis Johnson, Consul General, Yokohama Branch, Office of the U.S. Political Adviser
subfiles.summary: U.S. Consul General U. Alexis Johnson reports from Yokohama on the establishment of the Peruvian Nisei Association of Japan at an inaugural meeting held in Tokyo on July 27, 1947. He notes the location of the association's headquarters in Tsunohazu, Shinjuku-ku, Tokyo, and mentions that Lima-born Fernando Abey was elected as its representative. Johnson transmits a copy of the association's constitution in Spanish so that it may be forwarded to the Peruvian government.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 456 from U.S. Political Adviser (Yokohama) on the Formation of the Peruvian Nisei Association of Japan

subfiles.about: The official Spanish constitution and bylaws setting forth the objectives, governance, and financial regulations of the Peruvian Nisei Association of Japan.
subfiles.from: Peruvian Nisei Association of Japan (Asociación de Niseis Peruanos del Japón)
subfiles.summary: Preceded by an official enclosure cover slip, this document contains the 22 articles comprising the constitution of the Peruvian Nisei Association of Japan. The statutes specify that the organization aims to promote mutual friendship, protect the interests of Peruvian citizens in Japan, and pursue cultural and scientific activities, while permitting participation by individuals from other Latin American nations. Article 7 explicitly prohibits the association from intervening in Japanese domestic or foreign politics, and subsequent chapters establish a Deliberative Commission, annual general assemblies, administrative divisions, and a schedule of monthly dues in yen.
subfiles.title: Articles of Association of the Peruvian Nisei Association of Japan (Estatutos de la Asociación de Niseis Peruanos del Japón)
subfiles.to: Office of the U.S. Political Adviser / Government of Peru

subfiles.about: The Acting Secretary of State instructs the U.S. Mission in Lima to transmit copies of the Peruvian Nisei Association's statutes to the Peruvian Government.
subfiles.summary: The Acting Secretary of State forwards a copy of Yokohama Despatch No. 456 along with its Spanish enclosure to the Officer in Charge of the American Mission in Lima, Peru. The instruction requests that the Mission deliver the enclosed documentation to the appropriate agency of the Peruvian Government, provided there is no local objection. This step highlights the role of the U.S. diplomatic service in facilitating administrative and protective communication between third-party governments and their nationals in occupied Japan.
subfiles.title: Instruction No. 1213 to the American Mission at Lima regarding the Peruvian Nisei Association of Japan
subfiles.to: Officer in Charge of the American Mission, Lima, Peru

subfiles.about: Official file carbon copy of Despatch No. 456 reporting the formation of the Peruvian Nisei Association of Japan.
subfiles.from: U. Alexis Johnson, Consul General, Yokohama Branch, Office of the U.S. Political Adviser
subfiles.summary: This page is a verified department carbon copy of Despatch No. 456 from U.S. Consul General U. Alexis Johnson in Yokohama, dated October 17, 1947. It records the transmission of the articles of association of the Peruvian Nisei Association of Japan and identifies representative Fernando Abey and the group's Shinjuku headquarters. The copy was retained in State Department central decimal files in conjunction with the instruction sent to the American Mission in Lima.
subfiles.title: Copy of Despatch No. 456 from U.S. Political Adviser (Yokohama) on the Peruvian Nisei Association of Japan

subfiles.about: A typed departmental copy of the 22 articles of association of the Peruvian Nisei Association of Japan.
subfiles.from: Peruvian Nisei Association of Japan (Asociación de Niseis Peruanos del Japón)
subfiles.summary: This four-page text is a clean departmental typed copy of the complete statutes of the Peruvian Nisei Association of Japan, prepared for official transmission and record. It replicates the original 22 articles governing membership qualifications, objectives of mutual aid and cultural cooperation, prohibition against political activity in Japan, deliberative bodies, and dues collection. The copy bears minor clerical transcriptions, such as a typographical heading misprint ('Miseis'), while maintaining the legal framework established at the July 1947 Tokyo meeting.
subfiles.title: Copy of Articles of Association of the Peruvian Nisei Association of Japan

subfiles.about: White House Secretary Charles G. Ross refers Shujiro Iwasaki's letter addressed to President Truman to the Department of State for appropriate handling.
subfiles.from: Charles G. Ross, Secretary to the President
subfiles.summary: Charles G. Ross, Secretary to President Harry S. Truman, refers an incoming letter from Tokyo to the Department of State for official attention and appropriate handling. The referral slip is dated March 3, 1948, and was routed to the Division of Northeast Asian Affairs, where it was stamped as received on March 8, 1948.
subfiles.title: White House Referral Slip Transferring Letter of Shujiro Iwasaki to the Department of State

subfiles.about: Shujiro Iwasaki expresses gratitude for U.S. occupation assistance, introduces the International Club in Tokyo, and requests American guidance to promote peaceful foreign trade.
subfiles.from: Shujiro Iwasaki, President, International Club, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Shujiro Iwasaki, President of the newly founded International Club headquartered in the Mitsukoshi Building on Tokyo's Ginza, writes directly to President Harry S. Truman. Iwasaki expresses heartfelt gratitude for American material and spiritual assistance under General Douglas MacArthur's occupation, portraying Japan as a helpless child needing American nourishment and Christian guidance to recover from war devastation. He explains that the club was formed by international business leaders dedicated to reviving peace industries and foreign trade while spreading American democratic values among the Japanese populace, and he asks President Truman for suggestions and encouraging words.
subfiles.title: Letter from Shujiro Iwasaki (International Club, Tokyo) to President Harry S. Truman
subfiles.to: President of the United States (Harry S. Truman)

subfiles.about: The Secretary of State instructs the Acting U.S. Political Adviser in Tokyo to acknowledge receipt of Shujiro Iwasaki's letter to President Truman if appropriate.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of State transmits to the Acting U.S. Political Adviser for Japan in Tokyo a copy of Shujiro Iwasaki's letter of February 10, 1948, addressed to President Truman. The instruction suggests that the Political Adviser acknowledge receipt of the communication if no objections are seen locally. The document was drafted by Hillis Lory within the Division of Northeast Asian Affairs.
subfiles.title: Instruction No. 42 to the Acting U.S. Political Adviser for Japan regarding the International Club
subfiles.to: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo

subfiles.about: Counselor George A. Abbey reports on Japanese proposals to establish a Peace Construction Research Institute and explains why the U.S. mission advised against it.
subfiles.from: George A. Abbey, Counselor of Mission in Charge, Office of the U.S. Political Adviser, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Counselor of Mission in Charge George A. Abbey informs the Department of State that Koichiro Asakai of the Japanese Central Liaison Office visited the mission to discuss a proposal for establishing a Peace Construction Research Institute. Abbey reports that while the project's general research aims met with little abstract objection, the mission informed Asakai that attempting such an initiative before the promulgation of a formal peace treaty was premature. Abbey stressed that postponing the institute would not diminish its effectiveness and that additional time was necessary before the historical factors of the war could be evaluated with genuine objectivity.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 841 from U.S. Political Adviser (Tokyo) on Proposed Peace Construction Research Institute

subfiles.about: The formal prospectus, articles of incorporation, program of work, and estimated budget for the proposed Peace Construction Research Institute.
subfiles.from: Organizers of the Peace Construction Research Institute
subfiles.summary: This five-page enclosure sets forth the detailed foundational scheme for the Peace Construction Research Institute as a foundational juridical person based in Shiba-ku, Tokyo. The institute's mandate was to conduct comprehensive interdisciplinary investigations into the causes of the Manchurian Incident, the Sino-Japanese Affair, and the Pacific War, while documenting the loss of life, property destruction, and severe privations suffered by the Japanese population to ensure future peace. The document details the governance structure of directors, superintendents, and a 50-member board of trustees, along with a five-year operational plan (October 1946 to March 1951) and an annual operating budget of 239,650 yen funded primarily by government research commissions.
subfiles.title: Prospectus, Articles of Incorporation, and Budget of the Proposed Peace Construction Research Institute
subfiles.to: Japanese Central Liaison Office / Office of the U.S. Political Adviser
